why: A venue change for a trustees meeting with no link, no money and no data request; the only ask is to acknowledge, so acting on it carries no real risk.
Club newsletter from a long-established domain (2020) that matches the sender, and the sign-in is on the club's own site, not a lookalike.
A one-month-old sailing-association domain pushes a .docx attachment and link plus a 2,500 GBP sponsorship ask, dressed up with her sailing, firm and talk.
A 13-day-old domain asks for passport, proof of address, date of birth, CFA and director numbers before a mere intro call, which is identity harvesting.
Routine club lift-out logistics asking her to bring kit, with no link, payment or sensitive request.
Filing reminder from the registry's long-established domain (2009) with a modest standard fee filed on its own site and no lookalike link.
An 8-day-old domain claims a double booking deposit and asks for a manual bank transfer refund to a personal account, a classic overpayment-refund scam.
A three-week-old lookalike registry domain uses her public director number to drive her to a confirm-details link under a deadline threat.
The AV vendor's domain dates from 2020 and the message only offers a download of her own session recording with no credential or payment ask.
A 19-day-old lookalike of the podcast's domain sends an approve link under a Friday deadline, a phishing pretext built on her episode 41 appearance.
The host writes from the podcast's long-standing domain (2019) with episode stats and a link to the public episode page, asking nothing sensitive.
A recruiter on a domain from 2011 gives plain role terms, a no-login brief link and a phone number, and asks only for a call.
Sent from the forum's established domain (2012) with a no-pressure committee invitation; the newer 2027 event microsite link is only for viewing and nothing is requested.
A 17-day-old lookalike of the forum domain, sent deliberately to her personal address, pushes her to open an attached letter and complete an acceptance page under a deadline.
Renewal invoice from a data vendor on a domain from 2008 with payment details explicitly unchanged from prior invoices and no urgency or bank-change request.

A fake-reply thread from an unnamed research team asks for a one-click acknowledgement on a personalised link to unlock the client name, so she should verify the firm and the prior contact independently before clicking.
The booking vendor writes from its established domain (2016) to explain the newer status-page domain and states there is nothing to do.
A classic new-number family emergency text that discourages calling the old number, which is the opening move of a relative-impersonation money scam.
A named headhunter on a domain from 2018 describes a NED role plainly and asks only for her public biography, with no link, credential or money request.
An unknown temporary number claiming to be a colleague asks her to forward a 6-digit authenticator reset code, which is an account-takeover attempt.
Payment for the club winter series is routed to a seven-week-old off-site domain with an excuse for not using the club site.
Speaker expenses notice from the forum's established domain (2012) that sends her to its own form and explicitly refuses bank details by email.
An 8-day-old lookalike of her firm's domain sends an attachment to open and initial under deadline pressure, impersonating a colleague.
Race results from the sailing club's long-established domain (2008) with no request beyond the next race details.
An internal reminder from her own firm's domain pointing to the firm intranet form, with a known VPN caveat and no lookalike or unusual ask.
A colleague on a personal number urgently asks for a 9,500 GBP transfer to a new payee outside normal process, a textbook authorised-push-payment fraud.
A 13-day-old lookalike of the forum domain gates her delegate scores behind a form on that domain, a phishing lure built on her talk.
A 9-day-old lookalike of the trustees association domain demands an e-signature on an attached PDF under a voting-eligibility threat.
